title: The Global Water Crisis: Why We're Running Out

lines: Clean water from a tap seems endless.
But controlling water has shaped civilization.
Today, 7 in 10 people have running water.
Yet many cities face critical shortages.
slides.keyIdea: Access to clean water has been essential to human civilization and remains unequal today.

lines: Cape Town nearly ran out of water.
Day Zero: taps shut off for 4 million.
10+ major cities face similar crises soon.
By 2040, most regions lack year-round water.
slides.keyIdea: Multiple major cities worldwide are approaching water supply collapse within decades.

lines: Earth has 326 million trillion gallons.
97% is salt water. 2% is frozen.
Humans rely on just 1% freshwater.
Access depends heavily on geography.
slides.keyIdea: Water abundance on Earth masks severe freshwater scarcity for human use.

lines: Mexico City drained its ancient lakes.
Now it pumps groundwater unsustainably.
Aquifers took millennia to fill.
The city is literally sinking.
slides.keyIdea: Overuse of groundwater depletes ancient aquifers and causes land subsidence.

lines: Water consumption increased sevenfold this century.
Drinking uses only 8% of freshwater.
Agriculture and industry use the rest.
One hamburger requires 1,650 liters of water.
slides.keyIdea: Hidden water in food and products drives consumption far beyond drinking needs.

lines: Water is priced as if unlimited.
Farmers pay almost nothing for it.
Mexico City loses 42% to leaky pipes.
We waste water because it seems free.
slides.keyIdea: Underpricing water encourages waste and prevents infrastructure investment.

lines: Water scarcity drives violent conflict.
Darfur war linked to drought.
Syrian civil war partly caused by drought.
Competition for water intensifies globally.
slides.keyIdea: Water scarcity fuels geopolitical tensions and armed conflicts worldwide.

lines: Water is a human right, not commodity.
Higher prices hurt the poor most.
Cape Town cut usage 50% through conservation.
Recognize water's value before it's gone.
slides.keyIdea: Balancing water's value with universal access requires urgent individual and collective action.
